notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 109, drawn from the approved sources.

---

## Psalm 109 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### Overview and Structure

The psalm falls into clear sections: (1) vv. 1–5: plea for God to speak against lying accusers; (2) vv. 6–20: the imprecatory core — curses or prophecies of doom; (3) vv. 21–29: personal plea for deliverance; (4) vv. 30–31: vow of praise and confidence. All major commentators agree on this structure.

**Title and Authorship.** The superscription reads "To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David." Some think "Chief Musician" refers to the temple choirmaster; others take it as a poetic reference to God Himself as the author of music. Davidic authorship is widely accepted in traditional sources, though some modern critics date it later (Cheyne suggested the time of Nehemiah or close of the Persian age).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**The Imprecatory Problem.** Nearly all traditional commentators wrestle with the curses in vv. 6–20. Spurgeon calls this "one of the hard places of Scripture, a passage which the soul trembles to read." The Expositor's Bible states frankly: "It is far better to recognise the discordance between the temper of the psalmist and that enjoined by Christ than to try to cover it over." Yet all agree these are prayers *committed to God*, not acts of personal vengeance.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 1: *"O God of my praise, be not silent."*

**Traditional reading.** David begins by addressing God as the object and source of his praise. The phrase "God of my praise" means the God whom he continually praises, or the God in whom he boasts. The plea "be not silent" is a cry for God to speak — to act in deliverance — in response to the enemy's lying words. Calvin says David entrusts the vindication of his innocence to God in the face of calumnies. Spurgeon notes: "He only asks the Lord to speak: a word from God is all a believer needs."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

**Gill (Baptist).** Takes this as the Messiah speaking: Christ as man prays that the Father not be silent, comparable to Psalm 22:2. "O God of my praise" means God is worthy of all praise and was the constant object of Christ's praise while on earth.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

**Pulpit Commentary (Anglican/Evangelical).** If God makes no sign when men are grievously persecuted, He seems indifferent. Surely He will not treat one who praises Him continually in this way (cf. Psalm 28:1; 35:22; 39:12).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 2: *"For wicked and deceitful mouths open against me; they speak against me with lying tongues."*

**Traditional reading.** Wicked men speak wicked things, but the added layer is *deceit*. Spurgeon says: "In all Satan's armoury there are no worse weapons than deceitful tongues." David's reputation is being destroyed by slander. The "mouth" imagery is important — mouths are "opened" like a wild animal ready to devour.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

**Pulpit Commentary.** Calumny and misrepresentation are ever the portion of the children of God. David was calumniated by Saul (1 Sam 22:7–13), Absalom (2 Sam 15:3–4), Shimei (2 Sam 16:8), and others. One more perfect than David was even more calumniated (Matt 11:19; 12:24; 26:61).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

**Gill.** Applies this to Christ, whose enemies traduced His person, blasphemed His miracles, charged His doctrine with falsehood, and laid false charges against Him (Matt 26:59).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 3: *"They surround me with hateful words and attack me without cause."*

**Traditional reading.** The enemies encircle David with "words of hatred." The phrase "without a cause" is key — David insists on his innocence. This is the experience of the righteous sufferer. Both David and Jesus could say their enemies fought against them without cause (John 15:25).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

**Expositor's Bible.** Notes the contrast: lies and hatred ring the psalmist round, but his conscience is clear. "They have hated me without a cause" is the experience both of this ancient sufferer for righteousness' sake and of the Prince of all such.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 4: *"In return for my love they accuse me, but I am a man of prayer."*

**Traditional reading.** This is one of the most important verses in the psalm. The word "accusers" (or "adversaries") comes from the same Hebrew root as "Satan" (שָׂטַן, *satan*). David extended love to his enemies; they returned satanic opposition. His response? "But I am prayer" — the Hebrew is abrupt: *wa'ani tephillah*, literally "but I prayer." David's entire being was given to prayer; he became prayer as they became malice.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Spurgeon.** "He did nothing else but pray. He became prayer as they became malice. This was his answer to his enemies — he appealed from men and their injustice to the Judge of all the earth, who must do right."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html

**Boice (Reformed, quoted by Guzik).** "The Hebrew is more abrupt and therefore even stronger. It says literally, 'But I prayer.' That is, 'I am all prayer or characterized by prayer.'"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

**Ellicott (Anglican).** "I give myself unto prayer." Ellicott notes the psalmist means that in the face of all the taunts and reproaches, he simply and naturally has recourse to prayer — and, as the context seems to indicate, prayer *for them*.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/109.htm

**Pulpit Commentary.** "But I am wholly prayer — I do nothing during their attacks on me but pray for them."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 5: *"They repay me evil for good, and hatred for my love."*

**Traditional reading.** This sums up the complaint. David did good; they returned evil. He showed love; they gave hatred. This is the behaviour that sets up the imprecations that follow — it is not random rage but a cry for justice against calculated ingratitude and cruelty. The verse also prophetically prefigures Judas, who rewarded Christ's good with evil.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 6: *"Set over him a wicked man; let an accuser stand at his right hand."*

**Traditional reading.** Here the imprecatory section begins. David shifts to the singular, targeting the leader of his enemies. He prays that a wicked judge would preside over the man's trial. "Let an accuser stand at his right hand" — the right hand was the place of the advocate or helper in court; David prays instead that an adversary (Hebrew *satan*) would occupy that position. The Pulpit Commentary sees this as a calm, judicial sentence, noting that the spirit of Christian love must ever shrink from such utterances, which belong to an earlier dispensation (cf. Luke 9:51–56).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

**Ellicott.** Confirms the translation "Set a wicked man over him" is justified by Leviticus 26:16 and other passages. Notes that *Satan* here is "by no means a proper name, though the LXX and Vulgate have *diabolus*." The use of the same word in vv. 4, 20, and 29 points to the general meaning "adversary."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/109.htm

**Expositor's Bible.** Takes vv. 6–8 as describing a trial and condemnation before a tribunal. The word "set" is from the same root as "office" in v. 8, meaning to place in a position of judicial authority. The psalmist seeks vindication of public justice, not private revenge.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Gill.** Sees "the wicked man" set over Judas as Satan himself, who entered Judas and put it into his heart to betray Christ. "Let Satan stand at his right hand" — to direct, influence, and accuse.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

**A minority view (noted by Guzik, Spurgeon, and others).** Some expositors (Kennicott, Mendelssohn, Hammond, Westcott, G. Campbell Morgan) argue that vv. 6–20 are not David's curses but a *quotation* of what his enemies said about *him*. The shift to singular and the content of v. 20 supports this. However, most traditional commentators reject this view — Spurgeon says "we cannot for an instant accept it" — chiefly because Peter in Acts 1:20 quotes v. 8 as applying to an evil man (Judas), not an innocent one.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 7: *"When he is tried, let him be found guilty, and may his prayer be regarded as sin."*

**Traditional reading.** The trial ends in a guilty verdict — "let him go out condemned" (literally, "go out guilty"). The second half is among the most terrible imprecations in Scripture: may even his desperate prayer to God be counted as additional sin. The Pulpit Commentary calls this "the most terrible of all the imprecations." The idea is that the man's heart remains evil — his cry is not repentance but despair — so even his prayer is corrupt (cf. Prov 15:8; 28:9).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Ellicott.** Reads in the margin: "in his being judged, let him go out guilty." The condemned man's last cry to Heaven goes unanswered and is even counted sin.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 8: *"May his days be few; may another take his position."*

**Traditional reading.** This verse is the most famous in the psalm because the Apostle Peter quoted it in Acts 1:20 to justify replacing Judas Iscariot with Matthias among the Twelve. The Greek Septuagint rendered "office" (or "position") as *episkopēn* — "bishopric" or "overseership." The verse therefore functions both as an imprecation against David's immediate enemy and as a prophetic preview of Judas.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

**Expositor's Bible.** Peter's quotation does not make the whole psalm Messianic; it is a specific application of one verse by the Holy Spirit.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Spurgeon (Baptist).** The whole psalm refers to Judas, "for so Peter quoted it." But Spurgeon draws a line: "to ascribe its bitter denunciations to our Lord in the hour of his sufferings is more than we dare to do. These are not consistent with the silent Lamb of God, who opened not his mouth when led to the slaughter."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 9: *"May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow."*

**Traditional reading.** The curse extends to the man's family, reflecting ancient covenantal thinking where family solidarity meant consequences could cascade through generations. The short life wished for in v. 8 means orphaned children and a widowed wife.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Spurgeon.** "We are staggered to find the children included in the father's sentence, and yet as a matter of fact children do suffer for their father's sins, and, as long as the affairs of this life are ordered as they are, it must be so."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 10: *"May his children wander as beggars, seeking sustenance far from their ruined homes."*

**Traditional reading.** The consequences ripple outward: the orphaned children become vagabonds, driven from their desolate homes to beg among strangers. This pictures total social and economic ruin.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Gill.** Applies this to the children of Judas and to the Jewish people after the destruction of Jerusalem, when multitudes were dispersed as vagabonds begging from door to door.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 11: *"May the creditor seize all he owns, and strangers plunder the fruits of his labor."*

**Traditional reading.** The man's wealth is ensnared by creditors; everything he laboured for is plundered by foreigners. The Expositor's Bible notes this fits as a consequence of his sentence and execution — his estate is forfeit.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Gill.** Applies this to the Romans ("strangers" and "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel") who came into Judea, besieged Jerusalem, and seized all the Jews had laboured for.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 12: *"May there be no one to extend kindness to him, and no one to favor his fatherless children."*

**Traditional reading.** The man showed no mercy (see v. 16), so mercy is withheld from him and his children. Not a single person remains to show "lovingkindness" (Hebrew *chesed*) to his orphaned offspring.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 13: *"May his descendants be cut off; may their name be blotted out from the next generation."*

**Traditional reading.** The wish is for the complete extinction of the family line — the name blotted out, as if it never existed. This is the covenant curse of obliteration (cf. Deut 9:14; 25:19; Job 18:17).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 14: *"May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and the sin of his mother never be blotted out."*

**Traditional reading.** The curse now reaches backward to the previous generation. The sins of the man's ancestors are called to God's remembrance — not forgiven but brought to account — so that accumulated guilt falls on the present generation. This is a dread wish, but the Expositor's Bible notes it implies unrepented sins.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Gill.** Clarifies this does not refer to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (whose sins were forgiven), but to wicked ancestors whose sins the present generation filled up (cf. Matt 23:31–32; Rev 16:19).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 15: *"May their sins always remain before the LORD, that He may cut off their memory from the earth."*

**Traditional reading.** The sins stand perpetually before God as a legal case, not cast behind His back or buried in the sea (as forgiven sins are). The goal: complete excision of the family's memory from the earth.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 16: *"For he never thought to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and brokenhearted, even to their death."*

**Traditional reading.** Verse 16 is a turning point — the *grounds* for the curses. The man "remembered not" to show mercy (*chesed*). Instead of kindness, he actively persecuted the afflicted to death. This is not merely an enemy of David but an enemy of all that is good. Matthew Poole thought "the poor and needy man" was David himself.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Gill.** Applies this to Judas, who cared nothing for the poor (John 12:6) and showed no mercy to Christ, and to the Jewish leaders who persecuted Christ — the One who was "poor" for our sakes (2 Cor 8:9) and "broken in heart" (Ps 69:20).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 17: *"The cursing that he loved, may it fall on him; the blessing in which he refused to delight, may it be far from him."*

**Traditional reading.** The principle of poetic justice: the man loved cursing, so cursing comes to him; he rejected blessing, so blessing stays far away. This is not petty revenge but the outworking of a moral law — what a man sows, he reaps.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

**Spurgeon.** "Retaliation, not for private revenge, but as a measure of public justice, is demanded by the Psalmist and deserved by the crime. Surely the malicious man cannot complain if he is judged by his own rule, and has his corn measured with his own bushel."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

---

### v. 18: *"The cursing that he wore like a coat, may it soak into his body like water, and into his bones like oil."*

**Traditional reading.** The imagery is vivid: cursing was his everyday garment; now it penetrates him completely — like water saturating the inward parts, like oil seeping into the very bones. VanGemeren (Reformed, quoted by Guzik): "The wicked's love for cursing became so much a part of him that the psalmist describes it as if 'he wore cursing as his garment.'"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

**Expositor's Bible.** The curse "encompasses him" outwardly (robe, girdle), "passes into his inmost nature" (water), and "steals into every corner of his soul" (oil oozing into bones). The man is inwardly saturated with his own chosen evil.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 19: *"May it be like a robe wrapped about him, like a belt tied forever around him."*

**Traditional reading.** The curse clings to him permanently — like clothing that cannot be removed, a belt that never comes off. What he freely chose becomes his inescapable destiny.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

---

### v. 20: *"May this be the LORD's reward to my accusers, to those who speak evil against me."*

**Traditional reading.** This verse closes the imprecatory section by returning to the plural ("my accusers") and explicitly identifying these curses as the "LORD's reward" — i.e., wages paid by God, not human retaliation. David wishes and prophesies this doom, but it is God's work to perform it. The verse also confirms (for those who hold the traditional reading) that vv. 6–19 are David's own words, not a quotation of his enemies.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 21: *"But You, O GOD, the Lord, deal kindly with me for the sake of Your name; deliver me by the goodness of Your loving devotion."*

**Traditional reading.** A dramatic shift. "But You" (*we'attah*) marks the turn from imprecation to personal plea. David calls on God by the dual name "Jehovah, Lord" (Yahweh Adonai). He asks for deliverance not on the basis of his own righteousness, but for God's name's sake and because of God's *chesed* (loving devotion, mercy).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

**Expositor's Bible.** "Very pathetically, and as with a tightening of his grasp, does the singer call on his helper by the double name."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 22: *"For I am poor and needy; my heart is wounded within me."*

**Traditional reading.** David identifies himself as the "poor and needy" and "broken in heart" from v. 16 — the very one the enemy persecuted. His poverty is both material and spiritual.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 23: *"I am fading away like a lengthening shadow; I am shaken off like a locust."*

**Traditional reading.** Two vivid images of frailty: (1) the lengthening shadow at evening — about to disappear into darkness; (2) a locust shaken off a garment — easily dislodged, helpless. The Expositor's Bible notes the word rendered "am I gone" occurs only here and implies *compulsory* departure — being whirled away by external force.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 24: *"My knees are weak from fasting, and my body grows lean and gaunt."*

**Traditional reading.** David's physical condition has deteriorated — knees buckling from fasting, flesh wasting away. The Expositor's Bible notes the Hebrew literally reads "has become a liar" or "faithless" — a picturesque way of saying David's flesh had become a renegade from its former well-nourished state. Others (Kay, Baethgen) translate "My flesh has shrunk up for lack of oil."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 25: *"I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they shake their heads."*

**Traditional reading.** The enemies look at David's sorry condition and despise him — shaking their heads in a gesture combining pity and contempt. This recalls the mockery of Christ on the cross (Matt 27:39; Ps 22:7).

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

---

### v. 26: *"Help me, O LORD my God; save me according to Your loving devotion."*

**Traditional reading.** A simple, direct plea. Like the Canaanite woman in Matthew 15, David simply asks for help, grounding his request in God's mercy (*chesed*), not his own merit.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

---

### v. 27: *"Let them know that this is Your hand, that You, O LORD, have done it."*

**Traditional reading.** David's motivation is not merely personal rescue but God's glory. He wants his enemies and all onlookers to know unmistakably that deliverance came from Yahweh's hand. This subordinates self-interest to divine vindication.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

**Spurgeon.** "Ungodly men will not see God's hand in anything if they can help it … but all in good time God will arise and so effectually punish their malice and rescue the object of their spite that they will be compelled to say like the Egyptian magicians, 'this is the finger of God.'"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

---

### v. 28: *"Though they curse, You will bless. When they rise up, they will be put to shame, but Your servant will rejoice."*

**Traditional reading.** The contrast between human curses and divine blessing is absolute. The enemies' curses are impotent; God's blessing prevails. David looks at the outcome in faith as already decided: the enemies rise up, but they end in shame; David ends in joy.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

**Expositor's Bible.** "There is almost a smile on the psalmist's face as he contrasts his enemies' curses with God's blessing, and thinks how ineffectual are these and how omnipotent is that."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 29: *"May my accusers be clothed with disgrace; may they wear their shame like a robe."*

**Traditional reading.** The clothing imagery from the imprecatory section (vv. 18–19, where the enemy wore cursing like a garment) is now turned on its head: the enemies are clothed — not in their curses but in *disgrace*. Their shame becomes their permanent covering.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

---

### v. 30: *"With my mouth I will thank the LORD profusely; I will praise Him in the presence of many."*

**Traditional reading.** The psalm ends with a vow of praise. David promises vocal ("with my mouth"), abundant ("profusely" — this Hebrew expression for "greatly praise" occurs nowhere else in the Psalms), and public ("among the multitude" — in the congregation) thanksgiving.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm

**Maclaren (Expositor's Bible).** "The psalm began with addressing 'the God of my praise'; it ends with the confidence and the vow that the singer will yet praise Him."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

### v. 31: *"For He stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from the condemners of his soul."*

**Traditional reading.** The psalm comes full circle. In v. 6, an accuser (*satan*) stood at the right hand of the wicked man to condemn him. Now, the Lord Himself stands at the right hand of the needy *to save*. The accuser is replaced by the Advocate. Kidner calls this "the complete answer." Maclaren compares: "It painted an adversary standing at the right hand of the wicked to condemn him; it ends with the assurance that Jehovah stands at the right hand of His afflicted servant, as his advocate to protect him."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-109.html

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill)
Both Spurgeon and Gill read the psalm as primarily *prophetic* of Judas Iscariot. Gill states that "the imprecations in this psalm are no other than predictions of future events" — not personal vindictiveness but foretelling of exact historical judgment. Spurgeon goes further: though the psalm refers to Judas, he refuses to put the bitter denunciations in Christ's mouth: "These are not consistent with the silent Lamb of God." The Baptist approach tends to treat the curses as prophecy rather than prayer-patterns.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html

### Reformed (Calvin, Boice, VanGemeren)
Calvin (quoted at length in the Treasury of David) argues David was "free from all inordinate passion" and "breathed forth his prayers under the influence of the Holy Spirit." He warns against three corruptions: selfishness, carnality, and foolish zeal. The Reformed approach generally treats the imprecations as legitimate prayers of the Old Covenant — judicial, not personal — that reflect zeal for God's honour. Boice emphasises that David never acted on these wishes; he left vengeance to God (Rom 12:19).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word)
Guzik takes a pastoral approach: the imprecatory psalms are genuine prayers, but "with the greater revelation of grace and truth that came by Jesus Christ, we understand that we are to pray for the good of our enemies, and not for their ruin." The emphasis is on committing the matter to God and caring more about His vindication than personal revenge. The Psalm is taken as David's own words, with the curses being "in the form of prophecies rather than immediate curses."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

### Lutheran/Evangelical (Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott)
Both the Pulpit and Ellicott commentaries acknowledge the acute difficulty. The Pulpit Commentary states plainly that "the spirit of Christian love must ever shrink from such utterances, which belong to an earlier and less perfect dispensation (comp. Luke 9:51–56)." Ellicott wrestles with the public liturgical use of the psalm: the curses are "not general … but levelled at a single individual," making it harder to reconcile with temple worship. Yet both treat the psalm as inspired Scripture and seek to understand it in its historical-redemptive context.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/109.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/109.htm

### Methodist/Holiness
The Expositor's Bible Commentary (Nicoll, representing broad evangelical scholarship of the late 19th century) is the most candid about the "discordance": "It is far better to recognise the discordance between the temper of the psalmist and that enjoined by Christ than to try to cover it over. Our Lord Himself has signalised the difference." Yet Nicoll insists the *substance* — zeal for the triumph of righteousness, faith that God is just — remains a part of Christian perfection.

## Other Views

### The "Quotation" Theory
Several scholars (Kennicott, Mendelssohn, Hammond, Westcott, G. Campbell Morgan) have argued that vv. 6–20 are not David's curses but a *quotation* of what his enemies said about *him*. The shift to singular, the content, and v. 20 ("this be the LORD's reward to my accusers") are cited as evidence. This would make the psalm a lament about slander rather than an imprecation. Hammond called this "by far the more natural and reasonable interpretation." However, Spurgeon and most traditional commentators reject it, chiefly because Peter in Acts 1:20 applies v. 8 to Judas, not to an innocent slandered man.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-109/

### Modern Scholarship (Peake's Commentary)
Noted in search results: Peake's Commentary calls Psalm 109 "further than anything else in the whole Psalter from the spirit of Christianity." It dates the psalm possibly to the time of Alexander Jannaeus (before 80 BC), citing resemblance to the Psalms of Solomon.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/psalms-109.html

### The "Iscariotic Psalm"
Gill notes that the psalm was "used to be called by the ancients the Iscariotic psalm." Both Gill's Exposition and the Treasury of David confirm that the Syriac version titles it with reference to Absalom and adds "but to us it expounds the sufferings of the Christ of God." The psalm was understood in early Christian tradition as pointing to Judas and the enemies of Christ.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/109.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-109.html

### Catholic/Orthodox
The LXX and Vulgate translate "accuser" (*satan*) in v. 6 as *diabolus* (the devil). Ellicott notes this but argues the word is not a proper name here. No Catholic-specific exegesis from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org was found within the search results available.
